brief.subject: Fake passport help sites, a debt relief ban, and register overcharges
brief.headline: FTC Targets Passport Impersonators and Shuts Down Debt Relief Scheme Aimed at Seniors
brief.dek: Regulators act on passport-service impersonators, a debt relief operation that targeted seniors and veterans, and alleged checkout overcharging.
brief.lede: The FTC says a passport-services operation used paid search ads to pose as, or appear tied to, the federal government. If you're renewing a passport, be wary of sponsored search results.

sections.heading: Passport Help Posing as the Government
bullets: The FTC sued GovAssist LLC, Entry LLC and Scott Zuckerman over an alleged passport-services impersonation scheme.
Paid search ads allegedly made the operation look official, so the top search result may not be the government.
The complaint also cites misleading promises and fake reviews, so glowing ratings alone don't prove a service is legitimate.
Before paying for passport help, confirm you're dealing with the actual federal agency, not a lookalike middleman.

sections.heading: Debt Relief Scheme Banned for Good
bullets: A federal court permanently banned operators of an alleged debt relief scheme after an FTC request.
The operation targeted seniors and veterans by impersonating banks, credit card companies and government agencies.
On October 14, 2026, the court entered a $106.8 million default judgment against the corporate defendants.
If a caller claims to be your bank or card issuer offering debt help, hang up and dial the number on your card.

sections.heading: Checkout Prices Higher Than the Shelf
bullets: The FTC and 20 states sued Dollar General, alleging register prices routinely exceeded shelf tags and ads.
Regulators say the practice ran for years and cost consumers millions of dollars.
Small overcharges add up, so compare your receipt to posted prices before leaving the store.

items.title: FTC and State Partners Sue Dollar General for Charging Consumers More than Advertised for Many Products
